alalal-c50818-d1e104.summary: Rubric of Article 26: whether angels are circumscriptible.

alalal-c50818-d1e111.summary: Introduces the question on Lombard's statement that created spirits in place are in some way local and circumscriptible.

alalal-c50818-d1e125.summary: First objection: Lombard seems to contradict himself, having said earlier that spirits are not circumscriptible.

alalal-c50818-d1e137.summary: Second objection: to be circumscribed is to have parts joined to the boundaries of place, beginning, middle and end; angels are not so in place. Nor will it do to say with Gregory and Damascene that created spirits are bodily compared with the uncircumscribed Spirit, since what is spirit in itself cannot be body relative to anything.

alalal-c50818-d1e176.summary: Solution with Damascene: angels are circumscriptible in a way, not simply: when in heaven they are not on earth, so 'circumscribed' here means defined in place. Alternatively, circumscription is by place, time or comprehension; angels are circumscribed by comprehension, since, per Augustine, we comprehend what we can see the limits of, as with any being of definite essence. God is circumscriptible in none of these ways.
claims: Angels are circumscriptible only in a qualified sense: defined in place and comprehensible by their finite essence.
God is in no way circumscriptible.

alalal-c50818-d1e233.summary: Reply to the second objection: spirit is never called body, but 'corporeal' can mean from bodily properties or from bodily nature. An angel is corporeal by property, sharing with body definition in place and circumscription by comprehension, not by nature; since these properties appear more clearly when angels are compared with God, the saints call angels corporeal relative to God.
claims: Angels are 'corporeal' relative to God only by sharing certain properties of bodies, not by nature.

alalal-c50818.summary: Article 26 reconciles Lombard's statements that created spirits are and are not circumscriptible. Following Damascene, Albert holds that angels are circumscriptible in a qualified sense: they are defined in place, being in heaven and not on earth at once, and they are comprehended by their finite essence, which has limits. They are not circumscribed by place in the strict, part-for-part sense, and God is circumscriptible in no way. The saints call angels corporeal relative to God because they share some properties of bodies, definite location and comprehensibility, not because they have a bodily nature.
claims: Angels are circumscriptible only in a qualified sense: definitively located and comprehensible by finite essence.
God is in no way circumscriptible.
Angels are called corporeal relative to God by shared properties, not by nature.
